newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.S state seeks to smash tobacco research groups.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.S state seeks to smash tobacco research groups.

text.p: New York State Attorney General Dennis Vacco on Monday said that the state's lawsuit against the tobacco industry was the first to seek the dissolution of two tobacco research groups.
They are the Washington-based Tobacco Institute Inc and the New York-based Council for Tobacco Research USA Inc.
He said that New York was able to use its not-for profit laws to seek this remedy.
He called the two groups "a front for publicity," alleging that they gave misleading research data to the public.

Vacco said that he had approached the tobacco industry last year seeking a settlement of his planned lawsuit for $656 million. However, he said in October the tobacco companies made a "laughable" counter offer of less than $5 million.

Lucia Valente, chief special counsel, who was involved in the talks with the tobacco industry, told Reuters that to her knowledge, New York State was the only state which had made a direct settlement proposal to the tobacco industry. "They had an attitude...that they just can't be beaten."

The suit was filed by New York State against R.J. Reynolds, a division of RJR Nabisico Holdings Corp, Philip Morris Co.s Inc, American Tobacco Co. and Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp, which is owned by B.A.T. Industries Plc, Loews Corp's Lorillard and Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett Group Inc.
Vacco, who spoke to reporters at a news conference at his Manhattan office, said that the lawsuit does not seek a specific amount of damages.
However, he said that if the state should prevail, the figure could be in the billions of the dollars, making the amount which he was willing to settle for "seem like pocket change."

The New York attorney general said he thought New York's lawsuit would have an impact on the success of the national litigation filed by at least 18 state attorney generals against the tobacco industry. "They have the biggest player on the street involved in these lawsuits now...This changes the tenor of the debate."
